name: The Violinist Argument
statement: Even if you woke up plugged into a stranger whose life depended on your body, you would not be obligated to stay attached.
statementAccent: you would not be obligated to stay attached
meaning: The violinist argument is a thought experiment by the philosopher Judith Jarvis Thomson, from her 1971 paper A Defense of Abortion in the journal Philosophy and Public Affairs. It is designed to show that abortion can be morally permissible even if one grants, for the sake of argument, that the fetus is a person with a full right to life. Thomson asks you to imagine waking up back to back in bed with an unconscious famous violinist who has a fatal kidney ailment. The Society of Music Lovers, learning that only you have the right blood type, has kidnapped you and plugged the violinist's circulatory system into yours so your kidneys can cleanse his blood. If you unplug now he dies; but in nine months he will recover. Are you morally obligated to stay attached? Thomson argues you are not: a right to life does not include the right to use another person's body without consent. By analogy, even a fetus with a right to life has no automatic right to use the pregnant woman's body.
mechanism: The argument's strategy is to concede the opponent's strongest premise and still reach a defence of abortion. Grant that the violinist, and by analogy the fetus, is a person with a right to life. Thomson then distinguishes a right to life from a right to be provided the means of survival, in particular the continued use of someone else's body. The violinist's need for your kidneys, however great, does not establish that he has a right to them; unplugging does not violate his right to life but merely declines to give him something to which he has no right. So bodily autonomy, the right to decide what happens in and to one's own body, can outweigh even another's right to life when that survival requires the non-consensual use of one's body. The move reframes the abortion debate: instead of turning solely on whether the fetus is a person, it turns on whether a right to life includes a right to use another's body. Critics press the responsibility objection, that voluntary intercourse, unlike being kidnapped, may create a special obligation, to which Thomson replies with further cases and the distinction between a Good Samaritan and a merely minimally decent Samaritan.

examples.text: You are kidnapped and connected to an unconscious violinist whose survival needs nine months of your kidneys; Thomson asks whether you are obligated to remain attached.

examples.tag: Right to life is not right to a body
examples.text: Thomson argues the violinist's right to life does not give him a right to use your kidneys, so unplugging denies him only something to which he has no right.
Critics note the kidnapping fits pregnancy from rape better than consensual sex, where voluntary action may create an obligation; Thomson replies with further analogies.

variants.name: The bodily-autonomy reframing
variants.text: The shift from asking whether the fetus is a person to asking whether a right to life includes the right to use another person's body, centring bodily autonomy.

variants.name: Good Samaritan versus minimally decent Samaritan
variants.text: Thomson's distinction between going beyond duty to save another and meeting only basic obligations, arguing the law cannot compel the former toward the fetus.

whyItMatters: The violinist argument is among the most famous and influential thought experiments in applied ethics, reshaping the philosophical debate over abortion. Its innovation is to grant the fetus's personhood and right to life and yet argue that abortion can still be permissible, moving the argument off the contested question of when personhood begins and onto the rights and duties that hold between persons, above all bodily autonomy. Published just before the Roe versus Wade decision, it framed decades of discussion about whether a right to life entails a right to another's body and about the limits of what morality and law can demand of us for the sake of others. Beyond abortion, it stands as a model of how a vivid analogy can recast an entrenched debate, and it remains a standard test case in moral philosophy.

limits: The violinist argument is a defence of the permissibility of abortion in a range of cases, not a claim that every abortion is on a par; Thomson herself does not argue it settles all cases equally. Its central analogy fits pregnancy resulting from rape most cleanly, and the responsibility objection holds that voluntary intercourse, unlike kidnapping, may generate a special obligation to the fetus, a challenge Thomson addresses but that remains debated. The argument also assumes the framework of moral rights and the distinction between killing and declining to sustain, both contested. So it is a powerful and influential contribution to the abortion debate rather than a decisive proof, and its analogical reasoning continues to be scrutinised for how far it extends.
misreadings: Thomson is not conceding that abortion is killing an innocent and defending it anyway in bad faith; she grants fetal personhood only to show that even then a right to life does not entail a right to use another's body. The argument does not claim there is never any obligation to sustain another; it argues such an obligation cannot simply be presumed from a right to life. And it is not refuted merely by noting that most pregnancies are not like a kidnapping; the responsibility objection is a serious challenge Thomson engages, and the debate over how far the analogy reaches is ongoing.
origin: Introduced by the philosopher Judith Jarvis Thomson in her 1971 paper A Defense of Abortion, in Philosophy and Public Affairs, to argue that abortion can be permissible even granting the fetus a right to life, because a right to life does not include a right to use another's body.
